title: gates/gateEvents has real enforcement code wired to transitionTask, but no CLI write path exists -- the enforcement is permanently inert (second occurrence of QCLI-251's shape)
description:
Found while investigating the inbound quest-web/orchestrator question about acceptance-criteria completion enforcement (see the companion task QCLI-252). The orchestrator explicitly flagged this possibility: 'if both turn out to be that pattern, the interesting question stops being either individual gap and becomes which other schema fields are decorative.' Ran a systematic audit of every TaskState field against CLI wiring; gates/gateEvents is the one other field that fits the pattern QCLI-251 established for blockers -- though the mechanism differs in an important way.

Unlike blockers (which has NO enforcement code anywhere, confirmed in QCLI-251), gates DOES have real, working, spec-documented, well-tested enforcement: domain/gates/gates.ts's blockingGatesSatisfied() is called from domain/tasks/tasks.ts's transitionTask() and genuinely blocks a terminal transition (task_terminal_transition_gate_blocked) when a blocking gate is unsatisfied; docs/specs/quest-cli-dependency-ready-set-and-blocking-design.md documents gates as a deliberate lifecycle-eligibility constraint on readiness too ('Gates remain lifecycle constraints: if a pending gate makes lifecycleEligibleToClaim false, readiness is false'); and test/integration/gates/gates.test.ts is a dedicated, substantial test file (220 lines, 4 tests) exercising the domain logic directly.

But there is no command anywhere in src/cli/main.ts that can define a gate, record gate evidence, or satisfy one -- confirmed by grep across the whole file (the only 'gate' hits are unrelated substring matches, plus one explicit exclusion: task edit-batch's managedKeys set literally refuses to let a raw patch touch gates/gateEvents, naming them 'Managed patch key' as if a dedicated path exists elsewhere -- it does not). The Backlog migration importer hardcodes gates: []/gateEvents: [] (backlog-public.ts:247-248), same as it does for blockers. Confirmed live: 0 of 250 real task records in this repository (active, completed, or archived) have ever had a non-empty gates or gateEvents array.

Practical consequence: blockingGatesSatisfied() always evaluates over an empty array in any real Quest workspace today, which is vacuously true (Array.prototype.every on an empty array), so the enforcement can never actually fire through ordinary CLI usage. The gate-blocking machinery is real, tested, and correctly wired -- it just has no way to ever receive the data that would trigger it. This is a stronger case than blockers for making the field writable rather than removing it, precisely because the hard, enforcement-correctness part is already built and tested; only a CLI surface (define/satisfy/evidence flags, and manifest/help coverage) is missing.

acceptanceCriteria.text: A design decision is recorded first: gates/gateEvents becomes writable via CLI flags (define a gate, record evidence, mark satisfied -- mirroring the existing domain GateDefinition/GateEvidence/GateEvent shapes and blockingGatesSatisfied semantics already implemented and tested), or the field and its transitionTask/readiness enforcement are removed as dead weight

If made writable: quest task edit (or a dedicated quest task gate subcommand) can define a blocking or non-blocking gate, attach evidence, and mark it satisfied, all actor-attributed like every other Quest write, and quest manifest/--help reflect the new surface

If made writable: task edit-batch's existing managedKeys exclusion for gates/gateEvents either routes to the new dedicated path or stays excluded with a clear reason, rather than silently refusing with no pointer to how these fields ARE supposed to be written

Regression tests cover defining a gate via the CLI and confirm quest task complete/task list --ready actually refuse when a blocking gate is unsatisfied -- proving the already-built enforcement fires for real, not just in gates.test.ts's direct domain-level tests

implementationNotes: Sharpened by the orchestrator (opum-agent), and recorded here because it changes how this should be read: the gap is not "gates lack a CLI write path." It is "a documented lifecycle constraint has never once applied." blockingGatesSatisfied() is real, tested, and named in docs/specs/quest-cli-dependency-ready-set-and-blocking-design.md as a deliberate lifecycle constraint on both readiness and terminal transition -- not a stub, not dead code by any surface reading. Its 220-line test file passes, in isolation, testing a mechanism that nothing in any real Quest workspace can ever reach. That is a materially more dangerous shape than QCLI-251's blockers: absent enforcement is honestly absent, but enforcement that exists, is tested, is spec-documented as deliberate, and is structurally unreachable reads to any subsequent auditor as a safety property the system actually has. Someone auditing quest for lifecycle guarantees would find gates, read the spec, read the tests, and conclude correctly about the code and incorrectly about the system's actual behavior. This is why QCLI-253 is prioritized ahead of QCLI-251 despite being filed after it.
